title: Allocate Minimum Number of Pages
directAnswer: Binary-search the answer — the maximum pages any single student carries. For a candidate cap x, greedily walk the books left to right, opening a new student whenever the running sum would exceed x, and count students. 'Can we finish within k students if nobody exceeds x pages?' is monotonic in x, so binary search finds the smallest feasible x in O(n log(sum)). The lower bound is max(book), the upper bound is sum(books).

remember.pattern: Binary search on the answer + greedy partition-count feasibility
remember.formula:
if k > n: return -1            # more students than books → impossible
lo, hi = max(books), sum(books)
while lo <= hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
    if canAllocate(mid):       # students needed with cap mid <= k ?
        ans = mid; hi = mid - 1    # feasible → try a SMALLER cap
    else:
        lo = mid + 1               # infeasible → allow a BIGGER cap
rules: Books are assigned **contiguously** — student i gets a prefix-block of consecutive books. That contiguity is what makes the greedy count a single left-to-right sweep.
Lower bound is `max(books)`, not 0: one student must carry the single largest book, so the answer can never be below it. Upper bound is `sum(books)`: one student carrying everything.
The predicate is **monotone increasing**: if cap `x` works (needs ≤ k students), every cap `> x` works too. We MINIMIZE, so on a feasible mid go **left** (`hi = mid − 1`) and record it.
Guard `k > n` up front → return **−1**. With more students than books, someone gets zero books and the allocation is undefined.
Feasibility counts the **students forced** by the cap: start a fresh student whenever adding the next book would exceed the cap, then compare the count to k. Bail early once the count passes k.
whenToUse: Split a contiguous sequence into k groups and optimize the worst (largest) group sum
The objective is MINIMIZE the maximum (or maximize the minimum) of group sums
You can count, in O(n), how many groups a given cap forces
The answer is a number in [max(element), sum(elements)]
antiSignals: Groups need not be contiguous → this becomes a partition/DP problem, not binary search on the answer
You must output the actual partition, not just its cost → still binary search, but reconstruct after
Element values can be negative → prefix sums aren't monotone and the greedy count breaks
k can exceed n and that's allowed with empty groups → redefine feasibility carefully
remember.takeaway: Allocate Pages is the canonical 'minimize the largest group' problem. Spot the contiguous-split + min-max signature and you instantly know the move: bound the answer by [max, sum], binary-search it, and check feasibility with a one-pass greedy group count. Painter's Partition and Split Array Largest Sum are the exact same algorithm with relabelled words.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you see that the answer (the max-pages value) is the search space, can pin the bounds at [max(books), sum(books)], and can argue the feasibility predicate is monotone before coding the binary search.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Setting lo = 0 instead of max(books), forgetting the k > n impossibility guard, or going the wrong direction on a feasible mid (right instead of left) because the min/max direction got flipped.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State 'feasible(x) is monotone increasing, I want the smallest true', justify lo = max(books) out loud, and note the O(n) greedy count is exact because the split is contiguous and books are non-negative.

problemStatement:
You are given an array `books` of `n` integers where `books[i]` is the number of pages in the i-th book, and an integer `k` — the number of students.

Allocate **all** the books to the students such that:

- Each student gets at least one book.
- Each student is assigned a **contiguous** block of books.
- Every book is assigned to exactly one student.

Among all valid allocations, minimize the **maximum** number of pages assigned to any single student, and return that minimum value. If allocation is impossible (`k > n`), return `-1`.
understanding: Cut the book array into k contiguous blocks. Each block's cost is the sum of its pages; the allocation's cost is the largest block sum. You want the cut that makes that largest block as small as possible. The output is one number — the minimized maximum — which is the tell for binary search on the answer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Must each student's books be contiguous?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Student blocks are consecutive in the array. That's what lets a single left-to-right greedy pass count the students a cap forces.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if there are more students than books?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Impossible — some student would get zero books, violating 'at least one book each'. Return -1 immediately.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the array be reordered?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. The order is fixed; you only choose where to cut. Sorting would change which blocks are contiguous.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why is the smallest possible answer max(books)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Whichever student holds the largest single book carries at least that many pages, so no allocation can push the maximum below max(books).

examples.explanation: Best cut is [12, 34, 67] | [90] → block sums 113 and 90 → maximum 113. Every other cut has a larger maximum (e.g. [12,34]|[67,90] gives 157).
Cut [10, 20, 30] | [40] → 60 and 40 → max 60. Cut [10,20]|[30,40] → 30 and 70 → max 70. Minimum maximum is 60.
Five students but only three books — at least two students would get nothing, so no valid allocation exists.

approaches.name: Linear Scan Over the Answer — Baseline
approaches.whenToMention: Open with this to show you've identified the search space (the page cap) and the feasibility check. Then note the scan range is sum(books), which is too large.
hints: The answer is some page cap between max(books) and sum(books). What if you tried every cap from max(books) upward and returned the first that works?
For a fixed cap x, can you count how many students you'd need? Walk the books, keep a running block sum, and start a new student whenever adding the next book would exceed x.
The first cap whose student-count is ≤ k is the answer — once a cap works, every larger cap works too. But sum(books) can be ~10⁹, so the scan is the bottleneck.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each candidate cap (up to sum(books)) triggers an O(n) greedy student count. That's O(n · sum) — acceptable only when the total page count is tiny, far too slow under the real constraints.
approaches.explanation:
First nail the reframing: you are not choosing books, you are choosing a *number* — the page cap that the busiest student is allowed to reach. That number lives in `[max(books), sum(books)]`. The lower end is `max(books)` because the student holding the biggest book already carries that many pages; the upper end is `sum(books)` because one student could carry every book.

**The feasibility check counts students.** Fix a cap `x`. Sweep the books left to right with a running block sum. Add the current book to the running sum; if that would exceed `x`, close the current student's block and open a new student starting with this book. The number of students opened is exactly the minimum needed under cap `x` — because the split is contiguous and pages are non-negative, packing each student as full as legally possible minimizes how many students you use.

**Why greedy-fill is exact, not approximate.** With contiguous blocks and non-negative pages, the running sum only grows within a block. Delaying a cut (keeping a student busier) never forces *more* students later; it can only ever help. So 'fill each student to the cap, then cut' produces the fewest students for that cap — a precise yes/no feasibility answer.

**Why we walk caps from low to high.** The first cap whose student count is ≤ `k` is the minimum feasible cap, which is exactly the answer. And we can be sure it's safe to stop there: raising the cap only lets each student absorb more, so it never increases the student count. That 'larger cap ⇒ never worse' fact is the monotonicity we'll exploit.

**Why we don't ship this.** `sum(books)` can be on the order of `10⁵ · 10⁴ = 10⁹`. Running an O(n) check up to a billion times blows the time limit. Since feasibility is monotone in the cap, binary-search the boundary instead of scanning to it.
approaches.insight: The observation 'a larger cap never needs more students' is the proof that `feasible(x)` is monotone increasing. That single fact is the license to swap the linear scan for a binary search — the only change is how you move through the candidate caps.

approaches.name: Binary Search on the Page Cap (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer. Frame it as 'feasible(cap) is monotone, so binary-search the smallest feasible cap'.
hints: You showed feasible(cap) is false for small caps and true for large caps, flipping exactly once. What finds that flip in logarithmic time?
Binary-search the cap in [max(books), sum(books)]. At each mid, run the O(n) greedy student count. If it needs ≤ k students, mid is feasible — record it and try smaller; otherwise try larger.
Because you MINIMIZE, on a feasible mid record ans = mid and move hi = mid - 1; on infeasible move lo = mid + 1. The last feasible mid is the answer.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The cap range spans sum(books), so binary search runs O(log(sum)) iterations, each doing the O(n) greedy count. Total O(n log(sum)). Computing lo and hi is O(n); space is O(1).
approaches.explanation:
Binary search on the answer applies whenever the answer is a number with a monotone feasibility predicate. Here both conditions hold cleanly.

**The monotonic predicate, precisely.** Define `feasible(x) = true` if the books can be split into at most `k` contiguous blocks each summing to ≤ `x`. We argued in the baseline that raising the cap never *increases* the number of students forced — a roomier cap only lets each student absorb more books. So as `x` rises from `max(books)` to `sum(books)`, `feasible(x)` goes `[F, F, …, F, T, T, …, T]`: false while the cap is too tight, true once it's loose enough, flipping exactly once. **The answer is the smallest `x` that is true** — the left boundary of the true region.

**The feasibility check is the same greedy count.** `studentsNeeded(x)` sweeps the books once, accumulating a block sum and opening a new student whenever the next book would push the block past `x`. Because the split is contiguous and pages are non-negative, filling each student to the cap before cutting yields the minimum student count for that cap — an exact predicate, which is the non-negotiable requirement for binary-search-on-the-answer.

**Driving toward the smallest true.** Set `lo = max(books)`, `hi = sum(books)`. Compute `mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2`. If `studentsNeeded(mid) ≤ k`, then `mid` is achievable, but a tighter cap might also work — so record `ans = mid` and search the lower half with `hi = mid − 1`. If `mid` needs more than `k` students, it's too tight — search upward with `lo = mid + 1`. When `lo > hi`, `ans` holds the smallest feasible cap.

**The off-by-one traps, named.** (1) `lo = 0` instead of `max(books)` doesn't break correctness but lets binary search waste iterations on caps that can't even hold the biggest book — and worse, if you forget to clamp, an infeasible-everywhere range can mislead. (2) Updating `ans` on the infeasible branch returns a cap that doesn't actually fit `k` students. (3) Mixing up the direction — this is *minimize the maximum*, so a feasible mid means 'try smaller', i.e. move `hi` left. Going right there returns a cap that's larger than necessary. Recite the invariant — 'ans is always a cap that fits within k students' — and the pointer moves fall out correctly.
approaches.insight: Notice this is the mirror image of Aggressive Cows: there feasible was monotone *decreasing* and we maximized (feasible ⇒ go right); here feasible is monotone *increasing* and we minimize (feasible ⇒ go left). Same skeleton, opposite direction. Internalize 'which side is true, and am I taking the first or last true' and every binary-search-on-the-answer variant becomes mechanical.

pitfalls: Setting lo = 0 instead of max(books) — searches caps that can't hold the biggest book.
Recording ans on the infeasible branch — returns a cap that needs more than k students.

edgeCases.behavior: lo = hi = 50; the single student carries all 50 pages → answer 50.
One book each → max block is 7. lo = 7 is already feasible, so the answer is 7.
k > n → returns -1 via the guard before binary search.

commonMistakes: Setting the lower bound to 0 instead of max(books).
Forgetting the k > n guard that must return -1.
Moving hi/lo the wrong way on a feasible mid — minimize means go left.
Treating the split as non-contiguous, which breaks the one-pass greedy count.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong lower bound
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The busiest student must carry at least the largest single book. Starting lo at 0 explores caps that can never be feasible and risks an off-by-one when seeding ans.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int lo = 0, hi = 0;
for (int b : books) hi += b;   // lo never raised to max(book)
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int lo = 0, hi = 0;
for (int b : books) { lo = Math.max(lo, b); hi += b; }

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the impossibility guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With k > n some student gets zero books. Without the guard, studentsNeeded never exceeds n and you return a bogus cap instead of -1.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
def find_pages(self, books, k):
    lo, hi = max(books), sum(books)
    # no k > len(books) check
    ...

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong direction on a feasible mid
commonMistakesDetailed.why: This problem minimizes the maximum, so a feasible cap means 'a smaller cap might also work'. Moving lo right here returns a cap larger than the true minimum.
